 Health Insurance Open Enrollment 2027: How to Find Affordable Coverage and Compare Plans
 Prepare for health insurance open enrollment 2027. Check deadlines, potential savings, deductibles, doctors and prescriptions before choosing coverage.
 By: Daniel Brooks 
 | 
 Editor: Matthew Reed 
 October 24, 2026, 21:00 WITA · 4 min read 
 Stethoscopes on a calculator illustrate the cost of health coverage. Photo: Marek Studzinski/Unsplash. Illustrative stock photo. 
 Aktualita.co — Health insurance open enrollment for 2027 is approaching, giving Americans who shop through the individual Marketplace an opportunity to review coverage before the new year. Finding an affordable plan requires more than sorting the results by the lowest monthly premium.
 The right comparison includes what you pay to keep the policy, what you pay when you receive care, and whether the plan covers the doctors and prescriptions you use. Eligibility for financial assistance can change the calculation substantially.
 Advertisement 
 HealthCare.gov currently lists November 1, 2026, as the start of enrollment for 2027 coverage. Consumers should confirm the timetable for the Marketplace serving their state, because state-run exchanges can follow different schedules.
 Know the dates that affect your coverage
 Under the timetable displayed by HealthCare.gov, December 15 is the deadline to enroll in or change a plan for coverage starting January 1, provided the first premium is paid.
 The site lists January 15, 2027, as the end of open enrollment. Selections made from December 16 through January 15 generally begin February 1, again subject to paying the first premium.
 Employer benefit enrollment and Medicare enrollment are separate processes. Do not assume that an employer's deadline or Medicare's December 7 deadline applies to an individual Marketplace policy.
 Outside the regular enrollment window, a qualifying life event may create a Special Enrollment Period. Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program accept applications year-round.
 Apply for savings before judging affordability
 The sticker price is not necessarily the price you will pay. A Marketplace application determines whether you qualify for a premium tax credit, cost-sharing reductions or other coverage options.
 Use your expected household income for the year in which you want coverage. If you are self-employed, changing jobs or expecting a different work schedule, last year's tax return may be a starting point rather than an accurate final estimate.
 HealthCare.gov says more accurate 2027 income and savings estimates become available November 1. Before that date, figures based on 2026 information should be treated as preliminary.
 An offer of job-based insurance also matters. HealthCare.gov explains that an employer plan considered affordable and meeting minimum-value requirements can prevent eligibility for Marketplace premium tax credits. Do not assume declining an employer offer automatically creates access to subsidies.
 Compare the annual cost, including care
 For each plan, calculate 12 months of premiums after any assistance, then examine the deductible, copayments and coinsurance. Check whether particular services are covered before the deductible is met.
 “The costs when you get care can have a big impact on your budget,” HealthCare.gov explains.
 Consider a hypothetical comparison. One plan costs $180 a month after assistance, while another costs $250. The second plan requires an extra $840 in annual premiums.
 If the second plan would reduce your expected covered medical bills by $1,200, its combined premium and treatment costs could be $360 lower. If you rarely use care, the result could reverse.
 These figures illustrate a method, not available 2027 prices. Use the Marketplace's estimated yearly-cost tool and the actual benefit documents to compare your own likely use of services.
 The out-of-pocket maximum provides another important measure for an expensive medical year. Check what counts toward it: premiums, excluded services and many out-of-network charges do not simply become covered because you reach that figure.
 Give Silver plans a careful look if you qualify
 Premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions solve different problems. The first reduces the monthly insurance bill. The second can reduce deductibles, copays, coinsurance and the out-of-pocket maximum.
 Income-based cost-sharing reductions generally require enrollment in a Silver Marketplace plan. Choosing another metal category can mean giving up that particular assistance even if you still receive a premium tax credit.
 A Bronze plan's lower monthly price may therefore be less attractive than it first appears. Compare the Silver option shown after the application has calculated your eligibility, rather than comparing unsubsidized prices alone.
 Check doctors and prescriptions by exact plan
 Look up your primary care doctor, specialists, hospital and regular medicines for each candidate policy. A provider may participate in one product from an insurer while remaining outside another product's network.
 Review the Summary of Benefits and Coverage, provider directory and covered-drug list. Ask about specialist referrals, authorization requirements and whether a prescription has a separate deductible or different cost-sharing tier.
 If ongoing treatment is central to your decision, verify participation with both the insurer and the provider's office. Keep notes of the exact plan name and the information you receive.
 Finish enrollment and confirm the first payment
 Before applying, gather household information, your current coverage details and a realistic income estimate. Make a separate list of providers, medicines and expected treatment so that those needs are not lost during price comparisons.
 Existing customers should update their applications and compare the new year's options rather than relying entirely on automatic renewal. A familiar plan name does not establish that its premium, benefits or savings calculation will be unchanged.
 After selecting coverage, follow the insurer's instructions for the first premium and confirm the effective date. Save the enrollment confirmation, payment receipt and benefit documents together. That final check helps ensure the policy you researched is the policy available when you need care.
